findings.claim: Image created with Google Gemini Pro
findings.issue: "Gemini Pro" is a Gemini model tier/brand rather than a precise current model version. It is acceptable as an informal tool credit and not misleading, but the current Pro offering developers can call is Gemini 3.1 Pro (the 3.x family is current as of October 2026). No change required; flagged only so editors are aware the generic 'Pro' label does not pin a specific version.

findings.claim: One token is roughly 0.75 words on average.
findings.issue: Accurate as a widely-used rule of thumb (1 token ≈ 0.75 words ≈ 4 characters in English). Worth knowing that newer tokenizers (e.g., Anthropic's Claude 4.7+) can produce ~30% more tokens for the same text, so the ratio is approximate and tokenizer-dependent — but the 'on average' framing in the draft is fine.

findings.issue: Verified as accurate: the DeepLearning.AI catalog currently lists 107 short courses, so 'more than 100' is correct. Noted only because this is a changing quantity tied to a specific date and should be re-checked on future edits; no action needed for publication.

newData.body:
A curated collection of the best places to learn more about AI, large language models, and the broader landscape. ### **Foundational Reading**

Attention Is All You Need — Original Transformer Paper

The 2017 Google research paper that introduced the Transformer architecture which underpins every modern LLM.

AcademicArchitecture

arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 ↗

The Illustrated Transformer — Jay Alammar

The clearest visual explanation of how transformers work. Essential reading for anyone wanting to understand the mechanics without heavy maths.

VisualBeginner-friendly

jalammar.github.io ↗

Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3 Paper)

OpenAI's landmark 2020 paper introducing GPT-3 and the concept of few-shot learning at scale.

AcademicOpenAI

arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165 ↗
### **Courses & Interactive Learning**

fast.ai — Practical Deep Learning for Coders

Free, hands-on course that takes you from basics to building real neural networks. No heavy maths prerequisites.

FreeCoursePractical

course.fast.ai ↗

Andrej Karpathy — Neural Networks: Zero to Hero

YouTube series by former Tesla and OpenAI researcher. Builds a neural network from scratch in Python. One of the best free resources available.

FreeYouTubeCoding

YouTube Playlist ↗

DeepLearning.AI Short Courses

A large catalogue of short, focused courses on LLMs, prompt engineering, RAG, and agents — more than 100 of them as of 2026-10-03 — many taught by Andrew Ng and built with industry partners like Anthropic, NVIDIA, Google, and Meta. Each short course typically runs about one to two hours. Most are free to start — the gate is usually an email address and a login, not a credit card — and DeepLearning.AI also offers longer paid courses and specializations. Pricing and what sits behind any paywall change over time, so check the course page for the current terms. Ideal for non-technical learners who want to start watching and experimenting quickly.

Mostly freeCourseBeginner-friendly

deeplearning.ai/courses ↗
### **News & Commentary**

The Batch — DeepLearning.AI Newsletter

Free weekly AI news and commentary from DeepLearning.AI, with a personal letter from Andrew Ng in every issue. It curates the stories that actually matter — new model releases, research, industry deals, and policy shifts — and explains why they matter, so readers can keep up without being misled by hype. Clear, balanced, and accessible for both beginners and experts.

NewsletterWeeklyFree

deeplearning.ai/the-batch ↗

Import AI — Jack Clark

Detailed weekly newsletter from Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic and, as of 2026-10-03, the company's Head of Public Benefit — a role he took on in March 2026 to lead the Anthropic Institute, the lab's in-house research effort on AI's societal, economic, and security impacts. He previously served as Anthropic's Head of Policy and, before that, as Policy Director at OpenAI. Running since 2016, it covers frontier research, policy, and the strategic AI landscape, and has well over 100,000 subscribers. The newsletter is free, with an optional paid tier; read it on its Substack, which is the canonical home for the archive.

NewsletterResearch

importai.substack.com ↗

Simon Willison's Blog

Practical, technically sharp commentary on LLM developments — how they actually work, what they are good at, and where they fail. Written by an independent researcher and open-source maintainer.

BlogTechnical

simonwillison.net ↗
### **Model Playgrounds**

Ollama — Run models locally

Download and run open-weight models on your own computer. Free, private, no API costs.

FreeLocalOpen source

ollama.com ↗

Hugging Face — Model Hub

The GitHub of AI models. Browse, download, and test thousands of open models. Essential reference for the open AI ecosystem.

FreeModelsCommunity

huggingface.co ↗
newData.title: Interesting Resources

findings.claim: GPT-6 Astra ... released by OpenAI on September 3, 2026
findings.issue: September 3, 2026 was the limited preview/announcement date; the stable general-public release of Astra was September 4, 2026. Sources use both dates, with Sep 3 as announcement/limited preview and Sep 4 as stable public release. Not misleading enough to block, but the content could note Sep 3 was the preview and Sep 4 the public release.

findings.claim: OpenAI's current flagship is GPT-6 Astra (stated with no 'as of' date)
findings.issue: The 'flagship = Astra' claim remains correct as of today (2026-10-03): GPT-6.1 Sol launched Sep 29, 2026 as a mid-tier replacement for GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Astra was reportedly shelved, so Astra is still the top model. However, the card omits GPT-6.1 Sol entirely and lists 'GPT-6 Sol' as current when GPT-6 Sol has since been replaced by GPT-6.1 Sol in the API/Codex. Consider updating the model list and adding an explicit 'as of <date>' for freshness/robustness, though no house-rule 'as of writing/today' phrase is present so this is not blocking.

findings.claim: All six inline model links (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5) point to "#".
findings.issue: Every cited link is a bare "#" placeholder rather than a real destination, so the requirement to verify that cited pages exist and match their labels cannot be satisfied. This is not a factual error in the prose, but the placeholders should be replaced with real URLs before publication so readers reach the intended model pages.

findings.claim: "...the still-active Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5..."
findings.issue: Accurate as written, but worth knowing: Haiku 4.5 carries a near-term retirement floor of 15 October 2026 (≈2 weeks after today's date, 2026-10-03). It remains current/active now, so this is not blocking, but the page may need a prompt update if/when Haiku 4.5 is retired or a Haiku 5.5 ships (Anthropic has signaled a Haiku 5.5 is coming).

findings.claim: the more capable Gemini 3.1 Pro [as part of the] current generally available lineup
findings.issue: Gemini 3.1 Pro is the current Pro-tier flagship, but authoritative sources consistently label it as 'Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview' (preview stage), not full GA. The draft bundles it into a 'generally available lineup.' Correct framing: 3.8 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite are GA, while the Pro tier remains in preview (released in preview 2026-02-19). Not blocking because 3.1 Pro IS the current, callable Pro model and the lineup is not stale; the GA/preview distinction is a minor accuracy point that would not embarrass the site.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite for high-volume tasks [as the current Flash-Lite]
findings.issue: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (released July 21, 2026) is indeed a current, listed model, so this is not stale. Worth noting only that a newer 3.1 Flash-Lite / 3.5 Flash-Lite naming coexists in the ecosystem and other Flash-Lite variants exist; the named model is valid and current, so no correction needed.

findings.claim: The broader lineup includes Grok 4.3 and Grok 4.20 with 1-million-token windows
findings.issue: Grok 4.3 does have a 1M-token window, but Grok 4.20 does not — xAI documentation and OpenRouter list the entire Grok 4.20 family (reasoning, non-reasoning, multi-agent) at a 2,000,000-token context window. This is a specific, commonly-confused quantitative error; the correct figure for Grok 4.20 is 2M tokens, not 1M.

findings.claim: "models": "Grok 4.7 · Grok 4.6 · Grok 4.5 · Grok 4.3 · Grok Build 0.1"
findings.issue: The models list and the description are internally inconsistent: the description discusses Grok 4.20 (a real, current model) but it is absent from the models list, while Grok 4.3 appears in the list. Not factually wrong per se, but the lineup enumeration is incomplete/mismatched versus the prose. Grok 4.20 is a current model and arguably should be included.

findings.claim: Meta's frontier development has moved to its newer Muse line ... reflecting a renewed open-weight commitment rather than a move away from it.
findings.issue: This is factually backwards and is the kind of stale/inverted framing that would embarrass the site. Meta's frontier flagship, Muse Spark (1.3), is proprietary/closed-weights, and the Muse launch was widely reported as a strategic DEPARTURE from Meta's open-weight Llama tradition toward closed frontier models — not a 'renewed open-weight commitment.' Muse Spark was described as marking 'a sharp strategic departure from Meta's previous LLaMA model family, which had been released under open-weight licenses,' and Meta's 2026 frontier models ship behind a closed API. The open-weight Muse Glimmer is a smaller distilled/local model, not the frontier. The characterization should be reversed: Meta's frontier moved to proprietary models, with open weights now limited to smaller releases like Glimmer.

findings.claim: the open-weight, Apache 2.0-licensed Muse Glimmer (a ~30-billion-parameter model released August 10, 2026 that runs on a single consumer GPU)
findings.issue: Facts check out (30B, Apache 2.0, Aug 10 2026, single consumer GPU). Worth knowing: Muse Glimmer is a distilled/smaller model derived from Muse Spark and is positioned for local agentic workloads, not as a frontier model — the draft correctly separates it from the flagship but readers could misread 'open-weight commitment' as applying to the frontier line (see blocking finding).

findings.claim: the proprietary flagship Muse Spark 1.3 (released September 2, 2026, with a roughly 1-million-token context window)
findings.issue: Verified correct: Muse Spark 1.3 stable release is dated September 2, 2026, it is proprietary/closed-weights, and supports roughly a 1-million-token context window. No correction needed.

findings.claim: roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than 1.2
findings.issue: Accurate, but worth flagging that these are Meta's own self-reported engineering comparisons, not independently verified. Multiple sources attribute the ~20% fewer tool calls / ~25% fewer tokens figures to comparisons 'run by Meta's own engineers.' Consider framing as a vendor claim.

findings.claim: Muse Spark is the first model family from Meta Superintelligence Labs ... first versioned as Muse Spark 1.1 on July 9, 2026
findings.issue: Accurate, but note that the original April 2026 base model is sometimes cataloged as 'Muse Spark 1.0' by third-party trackers. The draft's phrasing (base 'Muse Spark' then 1.1) is consistent with Meta's own naming (Wikipedia: introduced April 2026, launched as 1.1 on July 9, 2026), so this is not an error—just a naming nuance that could cause reader confusion.

findings.claim: DeepSeek announced that from 04:00 UTC on September 14, 2026 all deepseek-v4-pro requests would route to V4.1-Flash at Flash prices... though it later indicated it may keep V4 Pro service running
findings.issue: This understates a confirmed, documented reversal as a tentative possibility. DeepSeek reversed the routing plan BEFORE it took effect (around Sept 11, with a change-log update seen hours before the Sept 14 deadline), stating it would continue providing V4 Pro API service after September 14, 2026 with billing unchanged. The newer official notice supersedes the old routing line. The draft's 'may keep... running' framing is weaker than the facts: as of early October 2026, V4 Pro remains live at unchanged prices and the Sept 14 routing never happened. The draft's advice to 'confirm current status directly with DeepSeek' is prudent and prevents this from being blocking, but the characterization is weaker than the record supports.

findings.claim: a 552B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model
findings.issue: Accurate for the backbone (552B total, 8B active prefill / 16B decode). Note that some trackers cite a larger total (~763B) when including ~196B Engram conditional-memory parameters. The 552B figure matches DeepSeek/SiliconANGLE reporting and is defensible; just be aware of the alternate total-parameter count if precision is challenged.

findings.claim: models: Qwen3.8-Max, Qwen3.7-Max, Qwen3.7-Plus, Qwen3.6-27B (open weights)
findings.issue: The open-weights model listed, Qwen3.6-27B, is superseded and presented as the current open 27B in a lineup led by Qwen3.8-Max. The current open-weights 27B is Qwen3.8-27B, released August 14, 2026 under Apache 2.0, which explicitly supersedes Qwen3.6-27B as the default local Qwen. Listing Qwen3.6-27B as the current open-weights entry presents a stale lineup as current — the pipeline's primary failure mode. Replace with Qwen3.8-27B.

findings.claim: the hosted model is available through providers such as OpenRouter and Together AI at roughly $2 per million input and $6 per million output tokens
findings.issue: Pricing and providers are correct ($2/$6 per million; Together is among the providers serving the open-weight Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B). Minor nuance: on OpenRouter the hosted flagship is the API 'Qwen3.8 Max' SKU while $2/$6 Together pricing is tied to the open-weight Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B variant; both land at $2/$6 so the claim is accurate, but the draft slightly conflates the hosted-API and open-weight SKUs.

findings.claim: roughly 95 billion active per token ... context window of up to one million tokens ... launched on August 3, 2026 ... 2.4 trillion total parameters
findings.issue: All verified correct (2.4T total / ~95B active MoE, up to 1M token context, GA August 3, 2026, open weights as Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B under custom Qwen3.8-Max License in mid-August). No correction needed; recorded only for completeness.

findings.claim: Mistral Medium 3.5 is the newest
findings.issue: Accurate within the three general-purpose LLMs listed (Medium 3.5 shipped Apr 29, 2026; Small 4 Mar 16, 2026; Large 3 Dec 2025). However, Mistral has since shipped later specialist releases (e.g., Leanstral 1.5 around end of June 2026, OCR 4.1 GA Aug 31 2026, Robostral Navigate July 2026). The claim is defensible as written since it scopes to this lineup, but 'newest' is only strictly true for the core LLM trio, not Mistral's catalog overall.

spotAuditFindings.issue: The tracker's newest OpenAI entries are the GPT-5.6 family (Sol/Terra/Luna), but OpenAI shipped an entire new flagship generation in September 2026: GPT-6 Astra (public GA Sep 4), GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna (Sep 22), and GPT-6.1 Sol (Sep 29, announced at DevDay). GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's current flagship and powers ChatGPT. Absence of any GPT-6 row would look like a clear oversight to an informed reader.

The tracker lists only Claude Opus 5 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5, but Anthropic has released a new 5.5 family: Claude Opus 5.5 (Sep 22, 2026) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Sep 28, 2026), with Opus 5.5 widely rated the current top coding model. This major Anthropic generation refresh is missing.
